Microsoft released an out-of-band update on November 25, 2026, to stop some Windows Server 2025 machines from crashing after installing this month's security hotpatch.

The crash is a stop error with code 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE) that occurs when IPv6 route timers expire on servers using Router Advertisement. Microsoft says the fix targets devices affected by the November 2026 Windows security hotpatch update, identified as KB5131077.

The emergency non-security patch is numbered KB5138318 and deploys automatically through Windows Update without requiring a restart of the affected servers.
items.title: Microsoft releases emergency hotpatch to fix Windows Server crashes

Anantha Nageswaran, India's chief economic adviser, warned at the Asia Future Summit that strong recent global growth rests largely on an artificial-intelligence investment boom that may already be deflating. He said much of this expansion has concentrated in one sector and its capital spending without reaching broad segments of the population, while also building financial-system vulnerabilities.

Nageswaran stressed the need to prepare for a post-bubble correction, arguing that AI productivity gains are not durable if they flow mainly to owners of capital rather than labour or workers who face displacement. He noted India's limited exposure to the boom could spare it from any hangover because Indian firms were largely absent among its major beneficiaries.

On China, Hutong Research partner Guo Shan said US restrictions on AI chips could bring forward a demand-supply rebalancing in that sector to 2027 from an earlier expected 2028. She estimated the limits could affect up to 30 per cent of chip-industry demand and would push China to accelerate domestic production.

Guo did not expect Beijing to launch another round of economic stimulus, saying China is still on track for its annual growth targets while the central bank focuses on fiscal prevention instead. She pointed to signs that China wants a more active global role through greater imports, sustained exports and overseas expansion by firms, likening it to Japan's 1980s trade rebalancing.

She tied these moves partly to renminbi appreciation, projecting stability over the next year but an increase of about 40 per cent toward 2035. The figure was offered as Guo's own forecast and is not a stated official target.

SGX chief executive Loh Boon Chye cautioned that diversifying investment portfolios does not necessarily diversify risks, warning that continued geographic concentration could raise risk even as opportunities exist across Asia.

Malaysia's economy minister Akmal Nasir said the country aims to capture more value from the AI boom by moving up the semiconductor supply chain beyond chip testing and packaging. He also noted greater scrutiny of data-centre investments over their energy and water use, with spillovers expected into building regional AI capabilities.

The Asia Future Summit took place on Nov 27 at Marina Bay Sands in Singapore for its fifth edition. It was jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu, sponsored by OCBC with Amazon Web Services as cloud partner.

As holiday shopping begins, consumers and workers are seeing how artificial intelligence is reshaping the retail industry. Anna, an anonymous Walmart cashier in southern Oregon who leads United for Respect, criticized the company's implementation of AI on the floor.

Anna said she receives at least 10 or 15 inaccurate safety alerts a shift that pull her away from customers, and that the system often mistakes shadows or stickers for actionable items. She called the technology unhelpful rather than supportive of workers.

In September 2026 several hundred Walmart workers signed an open letter urging the company to put workers first as it rolls out AI in stores. In June 2026 investors overwhelmingly rejected a proposal for a report on how AI and automation affect the workplace, though a cited internal survey found 84% of workers confident using digital tools.

A December 2025 National Retail Federation survey of 56 US-based retailers' AI leaders found most are implementing or planning to expand AI use. About 75% reported using it for coding and app development, 73% for office productivity tools, 66% for cybersecurity and fraud prevention, 59% for supply chain and warehouse operations, and 45% for marketing and advertising.

Labor leaders are calling for guardrails and regulations to protect workers and consumers. Crystal Weise of the AFL-CIO Tech Institute said AI-fueled surveillance is expanding across factories, warehouses, online shoppers, and store employees, and that such systems make jobs worse while raising prices.

Retailers including Macy's, Target, Home Depot and Costco use automated license plate readers at some stores to prevent theft and fraud. Wegmans, Macy's and Home Depot cite facial recognition technology, and Kroger archives customer data it collects and sells, per a 2025 Consumer Reports investigation.

Whole Foods uses an AI recruiting agent named Sage as the only way to apply for jobs there. Union leaders argue AI cannot account for life circumstances in discipline or termination decisions and can create pressure-cooker environments that they call algorithmic workplace harassment.

Fears of large-scale retail layoffs from AI have not yet materialized, though a July 2026 Stanford University policy brief found AI's impact on overall employment is likely small. In October 2026 Kroger announced plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs over three years citing AI use.

Kroger said the cuts aim to lower prices and improve operations; the company was also hit with a $2.6bn charge in 2025 after shutting down three automated robotic delivery centers. Union leaders say investors are pushing retailers toward AI investments that cut labor costs while squeezing workers and consumers.

Terry Engelder, a Penn State emeritus professor who estimated the Marcellus Shale held enough gas to meet U.S. needs for about 20 years at consumption rates in 2009, now fears natural gas has become a permanent energy source rather than the 'bridge fuel' he hoped it would be.

Engelder's estimate of 489 trillion cubic feet helped persuade banks to fund hydraulic fracturing that made Pennsylvania the second-largest U.S. gas producer behind Texas; critics say fracking harms health and emissions while stunting renewables.

He originally calculated the reserve hoping natural gas, which produces about 55 percent of coal's carbon emissions, would ease the transition away from coal toward wind and solar as he envisioned in a 2013 TED Talk.

His estimate was broadly confirmed by the U.S. Energy Information Administration in 2011 at 410 trillion cubic feet and revised upward to about 560 trillion cubic feet by the University of Texas in 2018.

Almost 60 percent of Pennsylvania's electricity now comes from gas, with demand expected to rise further as data centers are planned for the state.

Engelder said he calculated his figure using production data from Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia at the end of 2008; earlier estimates included an arbitrary 50 trillion cubic feet in January 2008 before a larger number.

He fielded calls from 512 reporters about his estimate, which he says still underlies industry assumptions today.

Engelder told Inside Climate News that gas would have been more of a bridge fuel if the country had maintained left-wing politics rather than pursuing 'drill-baby-drill' policies.

Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization founded in 2007 by two journalists who won a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting.

The MCS certification body recorded 269,195 UK solar installations below 50 kWp capacity in 2025, the strongest calendar year on record. Monthly data shows 260,131 solar installations were recorded in the ten months to the end of October 2026, with mid-November figures putting deployment ahead of that annual record.

MCS certification is not a legal requirement for small-scale installations in the UK, but it is typically needed to access utility export tariffs, so the measure serves as a strong indicator of residential and small-scale commercial rooftop deployment. Retrofit installations continue to lead in volume terms.

Installations on new build properties accounted for 31% of total installations in 2026, down from 37% recorded for 2025, though new build properties still represented approximately 81,000 installations in both years. MCS described the new build market as a key driver of solar growth and noted that England's Future Homes Standard will require almost all new homes to have solar panels by default from 2028.

MCS also reported record numbers of people investing in more than one technology for their home, reflected in small-scale battery deployment on course to more than double the annual record set in 2025. MCS recorded 73,115 certified battery storage installations to the end of October 2026, up from 41,460 certified installations in 2025.

Lisa Cooke, managing director of MCS, described the 2026 installation figures as 'incredible', saying they show how quickly the small-scale renewables industry is growing and leading the UK's transition to home-grown energy. Chris Hewett, chief executive of Solar Energy UK, said government finance support through the Warm Homes Loan Scheme should help further deployment growth.
items.title: UK small-scale solar installations hit a record in 2025

A strong El Niño coincided with sharply uneven October 2026 solar resource across South America, with irradiance above average north of 10°S and substantial deficits in the south-east. Analysis using the Solcast API found Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) about 4% above the 2007-25 average north of 10°S, but well below average further south.

The contrast tracked El Niño's typical rainfall pattern: drier skies in the Amazon and northern regions versus wetter conditions to the south-east. NOAA's Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.46°C for August-October 2026, above the +2.02°C recorded in the same period in 2015 and close to the later peak of the 2015-16 event.

North of 10°S rainfall was about 11% below average while roughly 84% of that area saw sunnier-than-usual conditions. GHI came in above average there, at 9% higher in Pernambuco, 5% higher in Ceará and 4% higher in Bahia.

In Brazil's four largest distributed-solar states irradiance fell well short of normal: about 19% below average in Paraná, 16% below in São Paulo, 7% below in Rio Grande do Sul and 5% below in Minas Gerais. Neighbouring Paraguay was also wetter than usual with GHI roughly 14% below average.

Deficits extended into Uruguay at about 10% below average and Argentina's Pampas at around 19% below, even though rainfall there stayed near or below normal. Central Chile was cloudier still, finishing about 28% below average after a month of heavy rain in Santiago.

Conversely northern Chile and Patagonia saw above-average irradiance, roughly 14% higher and 12% higher respectively, as weaker westerly winds carried fewer cloud-bearing fronts. Wildfire smoke near Manaus cut clear-sky GHI by about 7.5%, but drier conditions largely offset the effect to leave actual monthly values close to average.

Solcast produced these figures from satellite data and proprietary AI/ML algorithms at a global resolution of roughly 1-2km, with typical model bias under 2%. The company supplies irradiance models used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets worldwide.
items.title: Strong El Niño produced uneven October solar resource across South America

bp and Iberdrola have started operations at a 25 MW green hydrogen plant at bp's Castellón refinery, making it the largest operating green hydrogen facility in Spain.

The joint venture operates the plant to produce around 2,800 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually for direct use in refining processes that currently rely on grey hydrogen made from fossil fuels.

Iberdrola supplies about 170 GWh of renewable electricity each year under a power purchase agreement drawn from its Spanish wind and solar farms to run the plant.

The partners estimate the switch will avoid roughly 23,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually while reducing the refinery's associated carbon costs by replacing part of the grey hydrogen used in fuel treatment and impurity removal.

About 25 Spanish companies took part in the project supplying equipment or construction support, alongside the Instituto Tecnológico de la Energía (ITE), which received €15m from Spain's renewable hydrogen innovation programmes financed through the EU NextGenerationEU fund.
items.title: bp and Iberdrola launch Spain's largest green hydrogen plant

Women from ancestrally matrilineal ethnic groups across sub-Saharan Africa are substantially more likely to be living with HIV than their patrilineal peers, even though these societies traditionally grant women greater autonomy within marriage. The article argues that making routine, low-stigma HIV testing widely available could convert this latent risk into protective action.

The study combined laboratory-confirmed blood test results for roughly 150,000 women across 18 sub-Saharan African countries with historical ethnographic records to measure the effect (Loper forthcoming). In raw data, 11.6% of women from matrilineal groups were HIV-positive versus 3.5% among patrilineal women.

After controlling for education, wealth, religion, urbanisation and local development within the same province and survey wave, women with matrilineal ancestry remained 1.5 percentage points more likely to be infected, a 43% higher risk relative to the patrilineal baseline (Loper forthcoming).

The pattern appears cultural rather than geographic: female HIV prevalence jumped by roughly 2.3-3.3 percentage points across historical ethnic boundaries separating matrilineal and patrilineal homelands, with no similar jump for men, suggesting gender-specific social rules drive the penalty.

When matrilineal women migrate into patrilineal regions they carry their elevated risk profile; the effect is concentrated in high-prevalence East and Southern Africa epidemics and amplified further under Common Law property regimes. In West and Central Africa, where baseline prevalence is lower, kinship differences do not raise female infection rates (Loper forthcoming).

The mechanisms behind the penalty include greater marital turnover and partner change because a woman's children belong to her own clan with relatives as a safety net; reduced condom use since condoms require mutual agreement while women can independently use other contraceptives that prevent pregnancy but not HIV; and infections entering households through wider networks rather than from unfaithful spouses.

The reversal is diagnostic: among never-tested women, matrilineal ancestry was associated with lower condom use, but tested women who knew their status were significantly more likely to use condoms. The policy recommendation is routine testing during standard clinic visits or via self-testing kits in Malawi, Zambia and neighbouring countries (Loper forthcoming).

The author concludes that female empowerment is not a one-size-fits-all health intervention: without diagnostic clarity, autonomy within fragile marital contracts can inadvertently heighten exposure to HIV.
items.title: Matrilineal women face higher HIV risk; routine testing may help

The government will back legislation preventing wealthy or powerful individuals from using courts to silence critics, according to justice minister Sarah Sackman. She told parliament on Friday that Labour would support the private member's bill sponsored by Conservative MP Sir John Whittingdale.

Sackman said in a statement: 'Our legal system should be a route to justice, not a weapon of intimidation.' The bill aims to define abusive cases known as strategic litigation against public participation, or Slapps, so they can be dismissed early before defendants face unaffordable costs. She added that wealthy individuals often use the threat of expensive legal action to punish people even when they do not expect to win.

The government's decision follows an earlier announcement by prime minister Andy Burnham that changes would prevent non-disclosure agreements from hiding crimes. The debate has been reopened amid allegations against David Walliams, which he denies, and Russell Brand's conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Labour's support gives Whittingdale's bill a better chance of passing into law, but success is not guaranteed because most private member's bills are defeated or fail to secure parliamentary time. Even if it passes, campaigners say the bill does not go far enough and risks sitting on the statute books unused.
items.title: Labour backs bill to curb lawsuits used against journalists and whistleblowers

Macy's is reinventing itself as a luxury destination in an effort to win back shoppers after years of being crushed between discounters and upscale rivals. The department store, which has languished at the mid-price tier since before the pandemic, now counts Bloomingdale's and Bluemercury among its assets.

The company was squeezed by big-store costs, online competition, direct-to-consumer sales from brands, a shrinking middle class, and pandemic closures that pushed it to forecast $1.1 billion in losses (ev1) and knock it off the S&P 500 index (ev2).

A strategy of discounting everything failed over 2023 (dt3), when sales dropped almost 7% (ev4) amid soaring inflation that pushed lower-income shoppers to Walmart and Target while wealthier customers leaned toward higher-end stores.

In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over Macy's and announced a turnaround plan called 'A Bold New Chapter,' which included closing 150 stores (ev6) and upgrading more than 300 others (ev7).

Macy's reported growing sales in March after offering fancier options like real leather, Ralph Lauren, and Coach raised its average selling price by 9% in the latest quarter (ev8), with Bloomingdale's driving much of that growth.

The retailer insists it is not abandoning the middle class but adding elevated products across all price points. Consultant Michael Prendergast says breaking out of Macy's mid-tier reputation will be a hard climb, though he notes its 168 years make it one of the last major department stores still standing.
items.title: Macy's bets on luxury to escape its squeezed middle

An order of Papa John's margherita pizzas became the first purchase in the UK to be made by an AI agent using cardless payment technology. The transaction involved nine mini pizzas and was conducted as part of a Financial Conduct Authority regulated sandbox trial, working with Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

TrueLayer said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for goods on behalf of a real customer. According to its chief executive Francesco Simoneschi, the transaction required no account numbers or passwords and was handled at what he described as the highest possible security profile. The team ordered through Papa John's AI agent after giving it permission to access their bank account.

The payment used a strict mandate set with Lloyds that included maximum spend limits per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared. Simoneschi said the test was intended as the first step toward mass adoption of cardless payments by consumers.

Simoneschi predicted this could be 'the last Black Friday as we know it,' suggesting future AI agents will buy gifts on behalf of customers, manage finances, and help compare complex products. He added that good personal judgment still applies because such purchases require control and supervision while the technology is made fit for purpose under high security standards.

Simoneschi said consumers would remain protected by existing buyer's rights rules if an agent ordered the wrong product or made another error during purchase. Earlier this week, the FCA warned financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations.

Meta's personal AI assistant Muse launched in the UK on Tuesday and can also make online purchases, though unlike TrueLayer it makes payments using a customer's bank card.
items.title: AI Agent Makes Cardless Pizza Purchase: A First for UK

A recent study by Elaine K. Denny and Melissa N. Baker finds that receiving mental health counseling lowers the likelihood of protesting in subsequent weeks by 34% to 39%, according to analysis of a large national panel dataset.

The researchers report experimental results broadly consistent with these observational findings, including a field experiment showing mental health outreach reduces anxiety by an average of 11%.

Mediation analyses suggest that decreased anxiety is linked to reduced interest in political engagement. A separate survey experiment found higher anxiety associated with greater odds of volunteering.

AirAsia will delay staff salary payments until the end of each month from November through March to conserve cash amid steep losses, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

The carrier is Southeast Asia's largest budget airline. Its Philippine unit is also cutting jobs during this period.

Malaysian employees normally receive pay earlier in the second half of the month and will instead be paid on the 30th of each month, or the last day of February, throughout the five-month window.

The email was sent late last week by Chief People Officer Muhammad Khurram Zia and confirmed to Reuters by sources.
items.title: AirAsia Delays Payroll for Five Months as Losses Mount

The Netherlands will push back against proposed United States legislation that would tighten export controls on Dutch lithography giant ASML's sales to China, its trade minister said Thursday. Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma told parliament the government will do everything in its power to prevent the US MATCH Act from being adopted.

The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act seeks to align semiconductor export controls among the United States and its allies, but it has raised concerns over its potential impact on ASML and Dutch national sovereignty. Sjoerdsma said opposition was not a matter of party politics but 'a matter of national interest,' adding that the Cabinet opposes extraterritorial measures that undermine sovereignty in matters relating to national security.

Sjoerdsma argued the restrictions go too far because they also cover technologies that cannot be used to manufacture AI chips. He said the bill would hurt not only ASML, Europe's most valuable listed company, but also the tech sectors of other European nations. According to Reuters, he was working with the European Commission, Germany and France to prevent its passage.

Sjoerdsma stressed the Netherlands would continue opposing the bill even if it were adopted by Congress, saying 'even if the Act is adopted, we will seek to prevent it from taking effect.' China has long criticized the MATCH Act for overextending national security and abusing export controls. The Chinese Ministry of Commerce said the US bill would undermine the international economic and trade order and disrupt global semiconductor supply chains.
items.title: Netherlands Vows to Counter US Chip Bill Targeting ASML China Sales

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to become president of the European Central Bank, taking office amid deepening economic and political tensions across Europe. The Madrid-born economist was appointed just days before Spain's elections and will assume his role weeks before France votes.

The article frames De Cos as a pragmatic liberal centrist who believes markets function best when basic institutions work, while also recognizing that state and fiscal policy matter. He is described as the most technocratic ECB president ever, having built consensus during his tenure at the Bank of Spain and the Bank for International Settlements.

Sources in Frankfurt caution that he lacks experience managing serious crises—the very task awaiting him—while noting France poses an existential risk reminiscent of the euro crisis resolved by Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' approach. Analyst Alessandro Merli of Johns Hopkins warns De Cos will have a difficult job given supply shocks and high uncertainty.

France is presented as central to his challenge, with reports citing a projected deficit of 6% of GDP, debt levels at 120%, and risk premiums last seen during the euro crisis 15 years ago. The country faces possible fiscal austerity under far-right or far-left leadership from Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Inflation is reported to have climbed to 4% following an energy shock tied to wars, adding pressure on European economies as De Cos prepares for a potentially turbulent tenure.

Analysts say Asian governments could face hard choices between meeting Washington's latest tariff demands and preserving their economic ties with China, as existing free-trade agreements may offer little protection. The United States has proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, mostly in Asia, over alleged excess industrial capacity and unfair trade practices (ev1).

Vietnam could face a tariff of 35 per cent if negotiations fail, compared with 20 per cent if a deal is reached (ev2, ev3). Some countries might secure lower rates by concluding agreements with Washington.

Nathan Gray, senior research fellow at the University of Adelaide's Institute for International Trade, said the US appears to be seeking to reduce these economies' engagement with China rather than simply encourage domestic consumption. He warned that upsetting China risks most Southeast Asian nations because it is now their largest trading partner.

The Asia-Pacific Energy Transition Think Tank Forum 2026 took place in Hong Kong on Tuesday to discuss regional energy cooperation and the coordination of energy with computing power.

Co-organized by Our Hong Kong Foundation, the Global Sustainable Development Research Institute and the Hong Kong Green Energy Week Secretariat, the forum centered on two themes: Asia-Pacific Energy Cooperation and Governance, and Energy-Computing Power Coordination. The event aligned with China's APEC host-year theme of building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.

Opening speeches were delivered by Angelina Cheung Fung Wing Ping, Michael Williamson of ESCAP, and Yang Xin of the Development Research Center of the State Council. Cheung said Hong Kong is ready to serve as a trusted financing partner for the region's energy transition through its sustainable finance ecosystem and international carbon market. Williamson noted that no country can navigate the energy transition alone and described ESCAP's initiative promoting cross-border power grids, green investment and research to address rising electricity demand from AI.

Keynote speakers Radia Sedaoui of ESCWA and Xu Qinhua of Renmin University addressed two panel discussions on low-carbon resilient affordable energy systems and coordination of energy with computing infrastructure for efficient AI development. Participants discussed cross-border collaboration, energy security, grid resilience, financing mechanisms and the integration of electricity and computing resources.

During the forum, GSDRI inaugurated its Global Advisory Committee to advise on global resource connections and support the Belt and Road Energy Partnership. In closing remarks, Jane Lee said translating regional consensus into concrete action has become increasingly urgent following the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.
items.title: Asia-Pacific Energy Transition Forum Held in Hong Kong

Seagrass meadows provide vital marine habitats while capturing and storing carbon, but these underwater ecosystems are disappearing around the world.

Along China's eastern coast in waters off Shandong Province, a restoration project is working to reverse that decline.

Conservationists, scientists, and local fishermen have spent years attempting to bring lost seagrass meadows back to life.

The Path to Zero crew joined the effort to examine what it takes to rebuild an underwater ecosystem and how restoring seagrass could help combat climate change.
items.title: China Restores Lost Seagrass Meadows Off Shandong

A different kind of solar plant is designed to keep generating electricity long after sunset, addressing the challenge that conventional solar power stops producing when the sun goes down.

This type of facility uses tens of thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight and store energy as heat in molten salt. The stored heat can then be released to generate power when it is needed.

The Path to Zero crew traveled to Dunhuang in northwest China to examine how concentrated solar power could help solve one of renewable energy's biggest challenges.
items.title: Concentrated Solar Power Plants Store Sunlight as Heat for Use After Dark

Judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial have called on prosecutors to drop one case, seek a plea deal in another, and reconsider the third set of charges.

The prime minister is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust across three overlapping cases tied to his relationship with telecoms magnates and wealthy businessmen. Ending proceedings without a verdict could establish damaging precedents for media independence and holding politicians accountable.

Yael Freidson, Haaretz's legal correspondent who has covered the trial since 2020, said abandoning the case would leave 'the media to the whims of politicians and publishers' and set an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases. Netanyahu welcomed the recommendation as vindication, calling it proof that 'the truth has finally come to light.'

Attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara must now decide whether to accept the recommendations or continue a trial that has shaped Israeli politics for about a decade. Even if she proceeds, her ruling could be appealed and overturned by fresh judges.

The current bench had previously urged prosecutors in 2023 and again in 2025 to drop bribery charges but stopped short of recommending the whole trial end. The case has dragged on with testimony lasting more than a year and a half across 98 hearings, described as the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history.

The transcripts from all hearings run to more than 60,000 pages. Oren Persico of The Seventh Eye said he watched judges slowly lose control of their courtroom over that period.
items.title: Israeli judges urge end to Netanyahu trial

A vote to decide the fate of La Garnache's all-night church bells failed, with three-quarters of those who turned out voting for the chimes to continue.

The poll drew only 749 of the town's 5,515 residents. Organisers said this low turnout meant a quorum was not met, so an attempt to silence the bells did not succeed.

Since September 1942, the Notre Dame de l'Assomption clock tower has played an eight-century hymn every 15 minutes around the clock. Between 10pm and 7am it rings about 37 times each hour, totaling more than 700 individual chimes overnight.

Residents living near the church say the sound prevents sleep, especially during a heatwave with windows open. Thierry Simonin, who moved to his home in 2014, said he hears the bells ring roughly 726 times between 10pm and 7am.

Traditionalists defend the carillon as French cultural heritage. Former mayor François Petit, who organised the vote, argued newcomers should have researched life near the church before moving there. He also said the mechanical system of springs and weights cannot be easily switched off.

The dispute fits a wider pattern of rural 'noise nuisance' conflicts in France. A 2019 court ruling let a rooster keep crowing after holiday-home owners sued, and a law nicknamed the Maurice law was strengthened in 2024 to bar claims when pre-existing noise had not worsened for newcomers.

Uganda announced plans to withdraw its troops from Lubero in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours. The Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday that the troops would hand over security in the North Kivu province town to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations.

The withdrawal applies only to Lubero and does not affect Operation Shujaa elsewhere in DR Congo, according to Uganda People's Defence Forces spokesperson Col Chris Magezi. The UPDF were deployed to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces Islamist group fleeing joint military operations across eastern DR Congo.

Diplomatic tensions have escalated after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat over controversial social media posts by Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the president's son and Ugandan military chief. Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if rebels failed to do so.

The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as 'particularly serious' and demanded Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents. The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about civilian safety.

Despite a significant decline in ADF activities in Uganda since June 2025, the group remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled). Acled analyst John Ngono said the findings suggest Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC.

Ngono added that ADF is killing an average of four civilians a day and has expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo. He warned that the group's growing interest in mineral resources could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
items.title: Uganda Withdraws Troops From DRC Town Amid Diplomatic Row

items.summary:
Matt Handbury, a former media executive and nephew of Rupert Murdoch, admitted telling child sex abuse survivor Grace Tame she 'must be looking to be raped again' because of how she was dressed at an event. The remark has drawn condemnation after Tame revealed it in an op-ed for the independent outlet Crikey.

Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by her maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester from age 15. She was honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy on child safety. Handbury had not met Tame before their encounter at an event.

She wrote that she overheard Handbury speaking to a friend and confronted him immediately, then again later in the evening to confirm what she heard. The incident triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling as though she would vomit, with her body 'prickling in distress.'

Tame said none of the other seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and whistleblowers present intervened or took Handbury to task at the time. She described his remarks as especially egregious because they referenced a real, criminally tested traumatic experience rather than an imagined harm.

Handbury, 77, has not responded to a BBC request for comment but emailed Tame saying he regretted the 'highly objectionable' comment as soon as it was made. In that email he apologised for the 'attempt at humour in less than poor taste,' referenced her 'strikingly attractive get-up,' and thanked her for calling him out.

He wrote that no one could deny she looked fabulous, before signing off with a reference to discussing his behaviour with his therapist. Tame said Handbury's comment reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories, adding: 'How is that funny?'
items.title: Former Media Executive Admits Insulting Australian Child Abuse Survivor

items.summary:
Italian lawmakers are debating reforms that would make hunting the largest overhaul of the country's legislation since 1992 and recast hunters as wildlife managers. The bill is backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's conservative coalition ahead of a general election due in 2027.

The measures would let local authorities open more land to hunting, lengthen seasons, add previously protected species such as wild geese and pigeons to the list of targets, and introduce control measures for wolf populations. The Senate has already approved the bill; the Lower House began debating it this week with no vote date set.

Farming groups argue expansion is needed because wildlife damage to crops is rising, especially from wild boar. ISPRA estimated 1.5 million wild boars in Italy in 2021 and reported that agricultural damage averaged more than EUR17 million (US$18.6 million) a year between 2015 and 2021.

A 2025 survey by pollster Piepoli found 39 percent of Italians support abolishing or sharply reducing hunting, while 32 percent say it should be limited to genuine wildlife-control measures. Italy has around 430,000 registered hunters compared with roughly 900,000 in neighbouring France.

Environmentalists oppose the bill and staged a protest in central Rome on Nov 26. WWF's Luciano Di Tizio called it an archaic practice that should be consigned to history.
items.title: Italy weighs biggest hunting expansion in years, alarming wildlife groups

items.summary:
Efforts to combat malaria across the Southern African Development Community (SADC) have reached a critical point, with cases rising over the past two years as countries lose hard-won gains. At-risk populations are now more exposed than before, undermining the World Health Organization's goal of eliminating the disease by 2030.

Four regional countries—the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Angola and Tanzania—rank among the most affected in the world when measured by new cases per 1,000 people at risk each year. Together they account for 22.9% of the global malaria burden.

National programs are overwhelmed and under-resourced as unpredictable shifts in health financing compound the strain. South Africa stands out because it funds nearly all of its national program itself, whereas other countries depend heavily on external aid.

The World Health Organization set a target to eliminate malaria by 2030, which is now harder to reach amid these pressures.

A sudden suspension in 2025 of U.S. government funding for essential malaria activities complicated the Global Fund's goal of rebuilding its resources at $18 billion for its eighth replenishment cycle.

Global Fund allocations for the 2026-2028 grant cycle average about 18% lower than the previous cycle, forcing countries to choose which populations and areas to protect. Proven interventions that shield the most vulnerable are prioritized over less cost-effective ones, while elimination activities lose funding priority.

As a result of these shifting donor priorities, malaria cases rose in several countries including Mozambique, Nigeria and Uganda.

The La Niña climate event at the start of 2026 triggered severe flooding across SADC countries. It damaged essential infrastructure, displaced communities and contributed to rising malaria cases in Zimbabwe, Mozambique and South Africa.

Mozambique recorded a 55% increase in malaria cases during the first six weeks of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.

Zimbabwe reported 65,399 cases in the first quarter of 2026, nearly double the number from the same period in 2025.

Displaced populations frequently cross borders to reach essential services, adding pressure to already overloaded health facilities and raising the risk of medicine stockouts. In 2025, the International Organization for Migration and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees estimated about 11.4 million people were forcibly displaced in SADC, up 35% from 2023.

All SADC countries need effective early-warning systems and response plans to cope with extreme weather, unexpected population movements and surges in infectious disease. These tools should rely on rapid data sharing plus stronger regional coordination and cooperation.

A predicted 'super El Niño' could bring hot, dry conditions across southern Africa while heavy rains and flooding are expected in East and Central Africa. This may increase displacement and favor disease spread, underscoring the need for well-funded regional preparedness plans with effective coordination mechanisms.

Scientists have confirmed that recommended malaria treatments are becoming less effective in some regions due to genetic mutations of the parasite. Not all SADC countries have the capacity to detect and analyze these mutations.

Regional genomic surveillance hubs could quickly spot emerging drug resistance, but without proactive monitoring the risk of resistant strains spreading and rising mortality may grow. Qualified entomologists remain scarce despite training initiatives such as the E8 entomology scholarship program, limiting mosquito population monitoring and insecticide-resistance detection.

Experts say African governments should invest more in malaria control and elimination within their own countries to get the region back on track.

The extreme weather event at the start of 2026 refers to La Niña, which caused flooding across SADC. A predicted super El Niño is expected later, bringing dry conditions southward and heavy rains northward.
items.title: Malaria progress in southern Africa threatened by climate and funding cuts

items.summary:
The Zambian Supreme Court postponed for the fourth time an appeal by copper miner Sino Metals seeking to stop a community pollution lawsuit from proceeding. The adjournment, set on Nov. 18 with the next hearing scheduled for January 2027, follows an affidavit filed by Attorney General Mulilo Dimas Kabesha requesting more time to negotiate a settlement.

The dispute traces back to February 2025, when the tailings dam at Sino Metals' Leach Zambia Limited mine near Kalusale in Copperbelt province collapsed and released millions of liters of acidic mining waste into soils, crops, and waterways tied to the Kafue River system. In September 2025, 176 people from Kalusale and Chambishi filed a constitutional petition seeking compensation for the damage.

The plaintiffs also demanded environmental restoration and support for affected households, arguing their constitutional rights were violated by the spill. Sino Metals appealed on the grounds that a constitutional petition was not the correct legal procedure and that Zambia's Bill of Rights applies to private corporations only through the state; the High Court dismissed these objections before the case reached the Supreme Court.

During its June 2026 hearing, the Supreme Court allowed the Zambian government to join the case because it affects the wider public. In his affidavit, Attorney General Kabesha said 'substantial progress' had been made and quoted the government as actively working with all parties toward a comprehensive resolution of issues arising from the incident.

Some residents involved in the lawsuit report being pressured to move despite opposing relocation. Community members told Mongabay that Sino Metals has begun relocating them to Mutenda, about 90 kilometers (56 miles) from Kalusale, and started demolishing houses of those who moved there.
items.title: Zambian Supreme Court again delays Sino Metals appeal to block pollution lawsuit

items.summary:
Buenos Aires is holding 'Soup Kitchen Night,' a campaign by roughly 30 organizations to draw attention to police harassment of people gathering in public spaces and the growing number of homeless residents. The event comes as official data shows about 5,100 capital residents are homeless, though social organizations estimate the true figure is two to three times higher.

The situation has worsened amid an economic recession that fell short of growth expectations set by Javier Milei's administration at the start of the year. Official mid-2026 figures indicate 22% of Buenos Aires' residents are poor and 6.3% are extremely impoverished, meaning they cannot afford food; in absolute terms this amounts to about 193,000 people.

A UNICEF survey reports that families with dependent children reporting insufficient income rose by 10 percentage points in one year, bringing the total to about 2.7 million households across Argentina. Among these households, 43% cut back on food purchases and 36% postponed medical appointments due to lack of money.

The Buenos Aires municipal government has launched operations under banners of 'law and order' and 'order and cleanliness,' targeting street vendors known as manteros, informal parking attendants, and homeless people sleeping outdoors. These measures are applauded by many voters but increase the vulnerability of society's most marginalized members.

Activists say police harassment makes adapting to homelessness harder for those affected. Sol Lacava of Barrios de Pie, who organizes soup kitchens with other groups, says authorities demand a permit that does not exist just to distribute pre-prepared food and have arrested some organizers for complaining about the enforcement.

The campaign's visibility stems partly from this Wednesday's images of uniformed officers forcibly evicting customers from a café in Caballito. Social activist Juan Grabois used the incident to denounce what he calls the normalization of police repression against low-income residents, arguing that similar violence happens daily in working-class neighborhoods but goes unnoticed.

The municipal government responded differently depending on who was affected: it disciplined officers and launched an investigation into the Café Caballito eviction, while pursuing evictions targeting street vendors and homeless people. Graciela Lubo González, a 73-year-old retiree among those receiving meals Tuesday, said she could not sleep in shelters because of noise, illness, and uncleanliness.

González was evicted from her room two years ago after failing to pay rent and now receives a minimum retirement pension equivalent to about $220. She noted that only one in 10 Argentine women reaches the 30 years of social security contributions required by law upon reaching retirement age, and that unpayable debts have become one of the biggest economic problems facing Argentine households.

Hilaria Balza Ugarte, a Peruvian national who has spent nearly half of her 56 years in Argentina, said she voted for Milei expecting improvement but lost her job just before retiring. Her private school employer stopped paying staff and plans to close this December amid tax debt, forcing her into weekend eldercare work at reduced pay that could not cover rising rent.

Fabián, a 44-year-old kitchen assistant homeless for two months, said the current situation is worse than during the pandemic when his workplace sold takeout. His last restaurant closed recently and he has found no new job since moving to cheaper countryside housing, whose rent then rose unexpectedly. He reported that police took the mattress he slept on and socks a friend was selling near the plaza.

items.summary:
US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had urged Russian leader Vladimir Putin to end all military aggression against territories throughout Europe. Trump did not provide further details on the request.

He added that he hoped ending this aggression would help pave the way for a peace deal between Kyiv and Moscow.

Earlier Wednesday, Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand the war in Ukraine after meeting at Trump's residence in Florida. The two leaders made these statements jointly following their meeting.

Turkey's defence ministry said Thursday that Ukraine's attacks on Russian ships in Libyan waters violated international law. Turkey called on warring parties to refrain from attacking civilian ships and respect international law.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of preparing for a new mass attack on Ukraine, citing information from Ukrainian intelligence.
items.title: Trump Urges Putin to End Military Aggression Against Europe

items.summary:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has asked Netflix not to air its first local Pakistani production, 'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo,' in India. The streaming giant had not yet responded as of the report.

The Hindu reports that two Indian cinema federations—the All Indian Cine Workers Association and the Federation of Western Indian Cine Employees—have called for a ban on the series. They cite last year's terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 25 Indians were killed (ev1).

An Asia Times writer criticized India's reaction as fear over Pakistani dramas' popularity, comparing it to George Orwell's '1984' (dt2) and noting that Bollywood itself has benefited from cross-border cultural exchange. The Balochistan Pulse suggested the ban stems from Indian anxiety about the popularity of Pakistani content.

Separately, Taiwan heads into local elections this weekend in 22 districts as voters choose mayors and council members amid China's sovereignty claims over the island (ev3).

The Taipei Times reports Premier Cho Jung-tai has raised alarms that China is averaging 2.58 million intrusion attempts per day against Taiwan's systems (ev4). The paper frames the elections as a test for President William Lai, the ruling DPP party and opposition KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun.

China-linked accounts are also targeting Meta's app Threads in Taiwan, which accounts for 10 percent of all Threads traffic on the island (ev5). Officials say they have flagged some 2,400 such accounts to Meta (ev6).

A separate Washington Post piece promotes 'freudenfreude,' taking joy in others' success. It cites a small US study from 2022 that found acts of kindness improved lives most among people with anxiety and depression symptoms (dt7).
items.title: India asks Netflix to block a Pakistani series amid cross-strait tensions

items.summary:
Australia were bowled out for just 108 against England in the third T20I at Brisbane, ending their innings with their lowest-ever home total. Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as the standout performer.

Liam Dawson contributed 3-16 to help England take a two-nil lead in the series. The visitors also made an early breakthrough when Mitch Marsh was caught for 11.

England's run rate climbed after Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper posted respectively 22 off 14 balls and 26 off 14, though both were dismissed in consecutive overs.

Nikhil Chaudhary scored 66 and 45 in his previous two innings but only reached 19 here after hitting Overton on the thumb with a drive. Ben Dwarshuis was run out for four runs by Phil Salt to seal Australia's low score.

Former coach Darren Lehmann said via ABC Radio that Australia would be looking for about 220, or more, in reply despite the setback.

England has played only two T20Is at the Gabba and won both. They beat New Zealand by 20 runs there en route to winning the 2022 T20 World Cup.

Australia hold a strong record at the venue with seven wins from eight completed matches, having not lost since being beaten by the West Indies in 2013. England also have nine ODI wins from 17 games at the Gabba.
items.title: England beat Australia by 108-run collapse to take a two-nil lead in Brisbane T20I

items.summary:
Suzuki Motor plans to begin domestic production of lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries for electric vehicles in October 2029.

LFP batteries use iron and phosphorus instead of rare metals such as nickel, manganese and cobalt. The company describes them as cheaper and safer than the ternary batteries that Japanese automakers currently favor because of their higher energy density and longer range.

Suzuki says producing these batteries aims to reduce procurement risks for materials Japan imports from a limited number of countries, including China. A company official stated they will build supply chains that do not depend on specific countries.

The battery maker intends to produce LFP cells in Japan for the first time and may also use them as household storage batteries. It plans to develop safe, energy-efficient technology together with Eliiy Power, a Tokyo-based manufacturer.
items.title: Suzuki Plans Domestic Production of Rare Metal-Free EV Batteries

items.summary:
Former NHK director Atsunori Kawamura has released a documentary about photojournalist Bunyo Ishikawa, the sole survivor among Japanese war correspondents who died covering Southeast Asian conflicts in the 1960s and 1970s. The film opens Nov. 28 at K's Cinema in Shinjuku.

Ishikawa is one of three Japanese photojournalists to become subjects of films about their deaths, alongside Kyoichi Sawada (1936-1970), featured in the 1997 documentary 'Sawada: From Aomori to Vietnam,' and Taizo Ichinose (1947-1973), subject of the 1999 biopic 'One Step on a Mine, It's All Over.'

Kawamura chose Ishikawa because his perspective as someone who survived was compelling. In an interview with The Japan Times at K's Cinema in Shinjuku, Kawamura said: '(Ishikawa's) unique perspective was really appealing to me as a director.'
items.title: Documentary 'Battlefield Bohemian' Profiles Photojournalist Bunyo Ishikawa

items.summary:
Robotic dogs made by Sony have been rehomed in hospitals and other facilities across Japan to provide companionship for patients.

Aibo robots, which first went on sale in 1999, are no longer in production; owners who parted with their units donated them to Tokyo-based Sony Group Corporation under an adoption program where the machines receive repairs and upgrades before being reassigned.

The robot barks, cocks its head, moves its ears, waddles toward people, acts happy when petted, and goes to sleep. Packed with sensors and digital cameras, Aibo is programmed to remember its name, the owner's face, and its surroundings.

Sony official Yoshiyuki Katsuno oversaw the program and said owners feel as though they are sending off a robot that has become like their own child. He added that Aibo encourages people to talk to one another and can help tired patients pick themselves up.

Katsuno stated Sony hopes to spread the emotional healing and human interaction that Aibo offers, while Jerry Wang of FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem said an endearing shape is preferable when seeking a soulmate because it fosters emotional attachment. Cuteness is valued in Japanese culture as 'kawaii', where being cute is seen as an endearing trait rather than weakness.

At a university hospital on the outskirts of Tokyo, Aibo helped with long waits for visiting patients and persuaded reluctant children to undergo examination, according to doctor Manabu Komori. He said it helps motivate child patients because going to a hospital is generally unpleasant.

The hospital also uses real dogs to help patients feel better, though those animals require care, food, and can be temperamental. Dr Komori noted that Aibo offers some advantages but was careful not to say the robot dog is better than real dogs.

Sony does not disclose the pricing or number of Aibo robots sold.
items.title: Sony Rehomes 1999 Robot Dogs in Japanese Hospitals

items.summary:
A video shows a Levski Sofia supporter appearing to perform a Nazi salute in the stands during Marseille's Europa League match against Bulgaria. The footage circulated online after chaotic scenes at the Stade Vélodrome, where flares and projectiles were thrown and rival supporters clashed before and during Thursday's game.

About 500 Levski fans occupied the away section when several Marseille supporters breached that enclosure around ten minutes before kick-off, apparently targeting Bulgarian supporters. Flares and other projectiles were exchanged between the groups, with further disturbances breaking out at half-time.

Five Levski supporters were hospitalized for eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder, while about a dozen Bulgarian fans were reportedly injured overall, according to Marseille police prefecture figures.

Marseille won 1-0 despite the violence. The disorder drew condemnation from French President Emmanuel Macron and Bulgaria's Iliana Iotova, as did Levski coach Julio Velázquez, who called the scenes 'unacceptable for football.'

The incidents overshadowed the European fixture and renewed concerns about spectator safety at international club matches.
items.title: Levski fan filmed giving Nazi salute amid Marseille clash violence

items.summary:
Hundreds gathered outside the University of Havana on Thursday to honor Fidel Castro on the 10th anniversary of his death.

The event took place against a backdrop of worsening economic hardship, with power outages and disrupted food production blamed on United States sanctions imposed earlier this year.

Fidel Castro would have turned 100 in August, but celebrations for that milestone were scaled back due to the crisis affecting Cuba over recent years.

Cadets at the military academy said Fidel's legacy will endure and expressed continued support for defending the Cuban Revolution.

President Miguel Díaz-Canel and other government officials attended the memorial alongside young officers, waving flags and chanting 'Hail Fidel' as Castro's life was displayed on a screen outside the building.

Castro led Cuba's 1959 revolution, pursued Soviet-style communism, resisted United States pressure for half a century, and fell seriously ill in 2006.
items.title: Cuba Marks Fidel Castro's Death Anniversary Amid Economic Crisis

items.summary:
IBM is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of roles in its IBM Consulting division, which employs more than 150,000 people.

The company said it joins US high-skilled visa programmes to address skill shortages but that participation has been declining for years as skill availability and client needs have changed. It declined to give further details on the decision.

Affected employees reportedly face a choice by year's end between relocating outside the United States or leaving IBM, according to posts on the anonymous platform Blind. One employee described being given about three weeks to decide, with roughly 90 days of severance for those who decline an overseas role and December 31 as their last working day.

The same employee said she was offered a choice between taking an 80 per cent pay cut to relocate to India or losing her job by the end of the year.
items.title: IBM ends visa and green card sponsorship for most consulting roles

items.summary:
RBI Governor Malhotra addressed the SME Finance and Investment Summit, calling on MSMEs to pursue scale through technology, innovation, free-trade-agreement access, and international markets while asking banks to preserve relationship banking alongside digital infrastructure.

Bank credit to MSMEs grew at a compound annual rate of about 19% over five years (Sep 2021-Sep 2026), faster than overall bank credit growth. The governor said this outpacing makes lending to the segment profitable, though he cautioned that data and technology should strengthen rather than replace personal relationship banking knowledge.

Malhotra noted government support has grown so MSMEs need not fear outgrowing benefits; the credit guarantee scheme was doubled to Rs 10 crore. He also said repayment windows can extend beyond 90 days, sometimes reaching 180 days plus an additional 90 days depending on buyer payment terms and bank agreements.

On scaling up, Malhotra cited one estimate that only about 10 per cent of India's large companies in 2022 had been MSMEs at any point after 2000. He contrasted this with higher shares elsewhere: Australia (44 per cent), Israel (42 per cent), Indonesia (31 per cent) and Poland (30 per cent).

For firms that find scale difficult to achieve alone, he suggested collaboration through clusters, common facilities and partnerships with anchor firms. He also highlighted RBI measures easing collateral constraints, simplifying working capital norms, classifying all MSME loans as priority sector, raising the no-collateral lending limit from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 20 lakh effective April 1, 2026 (the first revision since 2010), and allowing banks to lend up to Rs 25 lakh for units with a good track record.
items.title: RBI Governor urges MSMEs and banks to strengthen lending ties

items.summary:
Amazon workers and supporters are striking and protesting in more than 20 countries from Black Friday on November 27 through Cyber Monday on November 30, under the Make Amazon Pay campaign convened by UNI Global Union and the Progressive International. The global action demands that Amazon respect workers' right to organize and negotiate with unions everywhere it operates.

The protests span German warehouses, Poland, the US, Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Australia, Canada, Japan, the Philippines and South Africa. In Germany, union ver.di has called strikes at 11 Amazon sites, its largest single strike call ever, accusing Amazon of aggressive digital workplace monitoring—a claim an Amazon spokesperson in Germany denied.

The campaign comes two weeks after warehouse workers in British Columbia won what unions describe as the first binding union contract for Amazon employees anywhere in North America. On November 13, an independent arbitrator set a three-year agreement for about 800 workers at Amazon's YVR2 fulfilment centre that raises hourly wages to CAD 29 and adds up to 18 weeks of severance plus a week of vacation for long-service employees.

The deal was imposed after arbitration because Amazon refused to reach an agreement, following a provincial labour board finding the company ran an anti-union campaign. Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka called the arbitration improper and unfair and said the company would go to court if needed; an Amazon spokesperson countered that it offers strong pay and benefits from day one.

Campaigners point out that Amazon made a record $77.7 billion profit in 2025 and plans to spend $220 billion in 2026, much of it on AI and data centres. Workers have also won other gains this year: three Italian transport unions signed national agreements covering all 57 of Amazon's sites there, and the US National Labor Relations Board ordered Amazon to bargain with a union at its JFK8 warehouse—an order the company is contesting in court.
items.title: Amazon Workers Strike Across 20+ Countries During Biggest Sale Weekend

items.summary:
The Nifty has risen about 17% from its October low, but roughly half of the index's companies still trade below their 2023 valuation levels as the rally pushes prices toward fair value. PL Capital's Amnish Aggarwal said current valuations in 48% of Nifty 50 companies are lower than 2023 levels.

The headline index now trades at about 21 times trailing earnings, up from 19.3 times at the end of October and still below its median of around 22 times since mid-2021. Wright Research's Sonam Srivastava said the November rally has made large caps less cheap but not expensive.

The advance is supported by roughly 22% profit growth among Nifty companies in the second quarter, according to Srivastava, who also noted that the rebound has been concentrated with the Nifty Next 50 trading below 18 times earnings near its lowest level in five years. That gap between heavyweights and the next tier of large firms helps explain how a rising index can coexist with many stocks still cheaper than earlier levels.

Downside risks include falling EBITDA margins, higher interest rates and possible commodity price rises flagged by Nomura, alongside HSBC's warning of a sharper consumption slowdown from inflation or El Niño. HSBC said 67% of companies it assessed reported second-quarter results in line with or ahead of expectations.

Banks see selective opportunities rather than broad-based gains: SBI Securities points to reasonable valuations in private banks, capital markets, FMCG staples, IT, auto, construction and power; J.P. Morgan targets 29,000 for the Nifty by end-2027 on expected MSCI India earnings growth of 12% in 2026 and 14% in 2027 but warns elevated valuations leave a narrower margin for error.

The 'cheaper than 2023' comparison may help identify stocks worth researching, but it does not establish that those shares are undervalued today. The case for buying depends on whether earnings can keep pace with prices and whether investors stay selective as the index rises.
items.title: Nifty rally lifts valuations while many blue chips stay cheaper than in 2023

items.summary:
A US investigation into the alleged diversion of Nvidia servers to China has drawn scrutiny toward former Nvidia executive Jay Puri and his relationship with Super Micro's ex-chief growth officer Cenly Chen. The Wall Street Journal reported that the two dated for several years before marrying on March 7, 2026.

Puri previously led Nvidia's global sales operations and oversaw chip allocation, while Chen worked closely with a server maker's customers and had regular dealings with Nvidia. He now runs AI computing provider ChronoScale.

Chen told the Journal by email that he 'never had to rely on personal relationships for professional gain.' Both Nvidia and Puri declined to comment on its requests.

Super Micro disputed Chen's role, telling the Wall Street Journal that he did not manage Supermicro's overall relationship with Nvidia or procurement of Nvidia GPUs. The company said a multi-department process determined how it allocated Nvidia chips to customers.
items.title: Ex-Nvidia Executive Under Scrutiny Over Alleged Server Diversion to China

items.summary:
During Black Friday sales in India, both the older iPhone 17 Pro and its successor the iPhone 18 Pro are available at reduced prices, creating a price overlap that complicates value-driven buying decisions.

Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series this year at higher prices than before. The 256GB model started at Rs. 1,64,900, which is about Rs. 30,000 above the iPhone 17 Pro's launch price of Rs. 1,34,900.

Apple stopped selling the iPhone 17 Pro through its official channels after launching the new model, so retailers are clearing remaining stock while offering both phones at discounts.

Vijay Sales lists the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro at Rs. 1,56,490 in its Black Friday sale. Buyers using an IndusInd Bank credit card EMI get another Rs. 10,000 off, bringing the price to about Rs. 1,46,490.

At Reliance Digital, the 256GB iPhone 17 Pro is listed at Rs. 1,27,900. Paying with a Kotak Mahindra Bank credit card EMI cuts the price to as low as Rs. 1,18,307, roughly a 7.5 percent saving.

BigBasket sells the same iPhone 17 Pro model for Rs. 1,26,990 with quick delivery where available. Buyers can take Rs. 4,000 off with an AU Bank credit card or earn NeuCoins worth about Rs. 12,699.

The older phone costs about Rs. 29,000 less than the new one before bank offers, and sale prices plus discounts change frequently so buyers should verify final prices at checkout.
items.title: iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Both Discounted During Black Friday Sales In India

items.summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has flagged high-severity vulnerabilities in the WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business apps, advising users to update their software. These advisories cover both a security flaw affecting messaging platforms and separate critical flaws found in ASUS products.

According to CERT-In, the WhatsApp vulnerabilities affect Android versions prior to 2.26.35.74 and 2.26.17.4; WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.23.70 and 2.26.17.4; WhatsApp Business for iOS before v2.26.23.72; WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72 and 2.26.15.72; WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72; and WhatsApp for Windows before v2.3000.1032164386.258709.

The agency attributes the flaws to attachment spoofing, SQL injection, improper certificate chain validation, incomplete validation of AI rich response messages, and external ad-reply URLs. CERT-In states that an attacker could exploit them by sending a specially crafted message, attachment, or URL to a targeted device.

Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code, obtain sensitive information, bypass security restrictions, or manipulate application data on the affected system, per the advisory.
items.title: CERT-In Flags High-Severity WhatsApp Vulnerabilities

items.summary:
WhatsApp announced a feature that lets users buy and install data-only travel eSIMs within the app, sparing travelers from airport SIM kiosks and roaming charges. The service is intended to launch in select countries soon.

The process requires only a few taps after installation, supplying mobile data abroad while keeping the user's usual phone number for calls and chats on WhatsApp. It addresses situations such as sharing boarding passes or notifying family of arrival without access to local connectivity.

WhatsApp partners include eSIM providers Jio, Smart Axiata, Smart Communications, Verizon, with industry coverage also listing 1Global. The company said it will add more providers over time to expand destination coverage.

Users will see the purchase option in the app once their country reaches the feature, according to WABetaInfo, which reported an upcoming update adding a buy option on the account screen and availability on Android and iOS.

WhatsApp has not disclosed which countries will launch first, eSIM prices, supported devices, or an exact rollout date. The addition reflects WhatsApp's broader effort to handle more everyday tasks within the app.
items.title: WhatsApp Adds Travel eSIM Purchase Feature With Jio Among Partners

items.summary:
Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on November 27 that a trade deal with the United States is close to finalisation, even as he acknowledged major uncertainties remain. Speaking by video conference at an event in Mumbai, he asserted India would proceed with trade agreements despite these unresolved issues.

Goyal projected that an EU free trade agreement would be signed this year and come into effect next year around March or April 2027. He noted the US has proposed capping tariffs on Indian imports at 17 per cent if a deal is reached, though he did not confirm whether such terms are settled.

The minister highlighted India's trade performance, stating that exports of foreign exchange reserves exceed $700 billion and could reach $1 trillion this year. He pointed to nine free trade agreements covering 38 developed countries over the past four or five years as representing a GDP of $16 trillion.
items.title: India's Commerce Minister Says US Trade Deal Nearing Finalisation

items.summary:
The Calcutta high court on Friday quashed the appointment of Ritabrata Banerjee as leader of opposition in the West Bengal assembly, ruling that his recognition was unsustainable under law.

A bench headed by justice Krishna Rao directed speaker Rathindra Bose to reconsider and issue a reasoned order, with a fresh decision required within 10 days. The court also asked the speaker to reach a new decision on the matter.

Speaker Rathindra Bose had earlier recognised Banerjee as opposition leader after this year's assembly elections. Banerjee leads the rebel Trinamool Congress faction that broke away from the party led by former chief minister Mamata Banerjee and her nephew Abhishek Banerjee. The speaker also named Akhruzzaman as chief whip.

Veteran Trinamool Congress MLA Sovandeb Chattopadhyay challenged the decision in court, arguing neither legislator had legal right to hold their posts after an interim arrangement expired on October 18 without extension. He alleged both continued to enjoy state-provided privileges attached to their offices despite lacking legal authority.
items.title: Calcutta High Court Quashes Appointment of Ritabrata Banerjee as Bengal Opposition Leader

items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Friday ordered the Karthigai Deepam lamp to be lit again atop the disputed Deepathoon pillar, suspended the temple's board of trustees, appointed two retired judges as receivers, and handed security duties over to the CRPF.

A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi issued these orders after the Karthigai Deepam lamp was lit at the customary mandapam instead of the disputed Deepathoon pillar on Friday. The court had earlier permitted the ritual as a one-time interim measure on November 24, but the lamp was lit only at the Ucchi Pillayar temple's Deepa Mandapam.

The Supreme Court suspended the board of trustees of the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple and appointed retired Madras High Court judges Justice S Vaidyanathan and Justice V Parthipan as receivers to manage it. It also transferred security responsibility for the temple and Thiruparankundram hill to the CRPF.

The bench issued contempt notices to Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, Director General of Police (DGP), Madurai Collector and other officials over alleged violation of its November 20 order permitting the lamp lighting at Deepathoon. Observing that state executive authorities appeared to have acted on political instructions, the court directed the chief secretary to appear personally and file an affidavit detailing emails, phone calls and messages exchanged between officials.

The bench said 'the wilful non-compliance of orders of the Court, especially by the executive authorities, cannot go unnoticed and it has to be dealt with an iron hand.' It described the conduct as prima facie indicating administrative chaos in the state and characterized the actions as a brazen and wilful disobedience that was a calculated affront to both constitutional courts.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the bench appearing for the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) that temple trustees had informed the agency they received no instructions from higher officials regarding entry. The court clarified its orders were binding on the state, its officials and every religious institution, warning it would 'set right anybody trying to create constitutional chaos.'
items.title: Supreme Court Suspends Tamil Nadu Temple Trust and Orders Deepam Relit

Raul John Aju, a teenage Indian entrepreneur known as the 'AI Kid of India', posted an Instagram selfie with Russian President Vladimir Putin after meeting him at the AI Journey 2026 conference in Moscow.

Aju said he began making videos at age nine and described his first video as being made in a bathroom. He wrote that taking a selfie with Putin was something never in his wildest dreams, per Mint's Anjali Thakur.

At just 12 years old, Aju reportedly developed his first humanoid robot, marking an early milestone in his technology journey.
items.title: India's 'AI Kid' Raul John Aju Shares Selfie With Putin After Moscow Conference
